cards.back: The **build-up of atheromas** (fatty deposits) in artery walls. It narrows the lumen and stiffens the wall.
cards.hint: Think about what builds up inside the artery over time.

cards.front: Why does a narrowed artery reduce the oxygen supply to the tissues beyond it?
cards.back: A narrower **lumen** offers more resistance, so less blood passes each minute. Tissues beyond the narrowing receive less oxygen and glucose.
cards.hint: Compare a wide pipe with a narrow one carrying the same pump pressure.

cards.front: How can a ruptured atheroma lead to a clot that blocks an artery?
cards.back: The atheroma surface cracks, exposing tissue beneath the **endothelium** to blood. Platelets stick to it, forming a clot (**thrombosis**) that can seal the narrow lumen.
cards.hint: Start from what happens to the surface of the atheroma first.

cards.front: What happens first when the endothelium is damaged?
cards.back: The damaged area becomes inflamed and **white blood cells** move into the artery wall. This is the first stage of atherosclerosis.
cards.hint: Think about how the body responds to injury.

cards.front: How does a fatty streak grow into an atheroma?
cards.back: White cells take in cholesterol to form a fatty streak under the endothelium. Muscle cells and fibrous tissue gather around it, and over years it becomes an atheroma, sometimes with calcium salts.
cards.hint: Follow the order of events, starting with the white cells.

cards.back: A **deposit** in an artery wall made of cholesterol, dead cells and fibrous tissue, sometimes with calcium salts. It is also called a plaque.
cards.hint: Think about where the deposit sits in the vessel.

cards.front: Why can atherosclerosis go unnoticed for many years?
cards.back: It usually develops **without symptoms**. People often notice it only once blood flow has been badly reduced.
cards.hint: Consider when the narrowing becomes large enough to cause a problem.

cards.front: What is the lumen of a blood vessel?
cards.back: The **hollow central space** through which blood flows.
cards.hint: It is the space inside the vessel, not the wall.

cards.front: Why does a stiff artery wall cause blood pressure to rise?
cards.back: A stiff wall cannot stretch and recoil as the heart pumps, so pressure in the artery rises. This raised pressure can damage the endothelium further.
cards.hint: Compare an elastic tube with a rigid pipe when a pump pushes fluid through.

cards.back: The **formation of a blood clot** inside a blood vessel, which can block blood flow.
cards.hint: Platelets play a key role in this process.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say an atheroma usually blocks an artery completely?
cards.back: Atheromas narrow arteries **gradually**. Complete blockage is usually caused by a clot that forms on a ruptured atheroma.
cards.hint: Think about how fast the narrowing builds up compared with a sudden event.

cards.back: Any **disease of the heart or blood vessels**, including coronary heart disease and stroke.
cards.hint: Think about which organs and vessels the circulation serves.

cards.back: A condition in which the **coronary arteries are narrowed** by atherosclerosis, reducing the blood supply to the heart muscle. It may cause chest pain during exertion.
cards.hint: Think about which organ the coronary arteries supply.

cards.front: How does a clot in a coronary artery cause a myocardial infarction?
cards.back: The clot **completely blocks** the coronary artery, so the heart muscle beyond it loses its oxygen supply and dies.
cards.hint: Consider what heart muscle needs in order to keep contracting.
